candidateRows: If God exists and raised Jesus from the dead, then the Christian God exists, establishing the cumulative case's governing inference.
This states the decisive bridge from generic theism and the resurrection to the specifically Christian conclusion named in the motion.
Hunter begins his affirmative opening by previewing two arguments for God and a historical case intended to identify that God with Christian theism.
Libertarian human freedom exists, cannot be accommodated by naturalistic determinism, and is therefore best explained by God's existence.
This is the first announced affirmative argument for God and supplies an independent route from ordinary agency to theism.
Hunter contrasts libertarian freedom with determinism and compatibilism, associates atheistic naturalism with an exhaustive causal system, and appeals to the felt ability to choose otherwise.
Determinism would undermine meaningful moral responsibility and rational affirmation because actions and beliefs could not have been otherwise.
These consequences support the freedom premise by arguing that rejecting libertarian agency carries severe costs for morality and rational debate itself.
Hunter develops two implications of determinism: blame would lose its ordinary basis, and reasoning could not genuinely influence beliefs or choices among alternatives.
Because everything that begins has a cause and the universe began, its best explanation is a timeless, spaceless, immaterial, powerful mind.
This is the second principal route to theism, moving from the universe's beginning to a personal transcendent cause with divine attributes.
Hunter presents the causal syllogism, argues against an infinite past, and infers that the cause of time, space, and matter must transcend nature and possess causal power.
Replacing God with universe-creating pixies does not provide a genuinely different explanation, because parsimony reduces it to one being with divine attributes.
This protects the cosmological inference against a named alternative and argues that relabeling the inferred cause does not avoid theism.
Dillahunty's earlier contrary suggestion that universe-creating pixies could explain the universe instead of God.
Hunter applies parsimony to the proposed plurality of creators and contends that the remaining singular, transcendent, powerful cause is substantively what theists mean by God.
Prior reason to accept God and Jesus's claimed divine mission raises the antecedent plausibility of God resurrecting Jesus.
This supplies the methodological bridge that permits the resurrection case to overcome an initial objection based solely on its miraculous character.
Hunter argues that a resurrection would be highly unlikely without God, but becomes more plausible once a capable God and Jesus's special religious role are included in the background account.
Jesus's crucifixion, reported post-death appearances, and the disciples' costly commitment make divine resurrection the best historical explanation.
This is the principal specifically Christian argument and provides the asserted historical basis for identifying the previously inferred God with Christian theism.

Hunter appeals to broad scholarly agreement on Jesus's death and early appearance beliefs, challenges swoon and group-hallucination accounts, and invokes the disciples' willingness to suffer for their conviction.
Arguments equally available to many religions cannot establish the specifically Christian God, and skepticism need not assert that no god exists.
This directly challenges the affirmative case's religious specificity while defining the negative burden as withholding belief rather than proving universal nonexistence.
Hunter's earlier claim that his generic theistic arguments and resurrection case establish the existence of the Christian God.
Dillahunty distinguishes atheistic nonbelief from a universal denial of gods and argues that premises usable by competing faiths do not discriminate in favor of Christianity.
Historical conclusions require comparative background support and may remain uncertain, while an unrestricted divine explanation lacks discriminatory explanatory force.
It establishes the negative side's governing epistemic standard and begins applying it against the affirmative's inference from unusual historical claims to divine action.
Hunter's earlier contention that divine resurrection is the best historical explanation of the reported events surrounding Jesus.

Dillahunty uses ordinary inference examples to stress background frequencies, fallibility, and suspended judgment, then argues that divine action can be invoked for almost anything and is difficult to distinguish from magic.
Treating God as a universal best explanation supplies no discriminating explanatory power because it is indistinguishable from magic or invented alternatives.
This challenges the explanatory foundation of the cumulative theistic case by arguing that an explanation compatible with virtually every outcome confirms nothing distinctive.
The earlier pro position that God is the best causal explanation for features of reality.
After discussing fallible inference, Dillahunty argues that merely invoking God can answer almost any question and therefore cannot distinguish theism from magic.
Religious claims require a method that reliably selects one hypothesis over competing religions rather than reproducing mutually incompatible conclusions.
This establishes the skeptical standard applied throughout the debate and directly contests whether the Christian cumulative case uniquely warrants its conclusion.
Dillahunty traces religions through human testimony and error, applies skepticism to his former faith, and demands a consistently discriminating epistemic methodology.
A God who wants people to know him should generate observable expectations, so pervasive reasonable nonbelief is substantial disconfirming evidence for that God model.
Divine hiddenness is one of the debate's named central issues and bears directly on whether the Christian God's alleged aims fit the observed world.
He frames God models as prediction-generating hypotheses and argues that absent expected signs count against a clarity-seeking God without deductively disproving one.
Competing and internally divided revelations undermine Christianity because believers identify errors in rival traditions without applying the same skepticism to their own.
Inconsistent revelation is a named central route in the motion and challenges both Christianity's distinctiveness and the claimed clarity of divine communication.
Dillahunty links reasonable nonbelief to disagreements among denominations and religions, then contrasts claimed revelation with his sincere but unanswered search for guidance.
Even spectacular apparent miracles would not uniquely establish God because advanced intelligence, deception, or unknown mechanisms could produce the same observations.
This explains the skeptic's evidential threshold and blocks an inference from astonishing unexplained events directly to the specifically Christian supernatural explanation.
Considering what might convince him, Dillahunty distinguishes extraordinary phenomena from their cause and uses stage magic to illustrate how confidently observers can misattribute effects.
No available method reliably points to any God, while a truth-seeking Christian God should communicate more clearly than through an ancient, altered, disputed story.
This synthesizes the methodological, hiddenness, and revelation objections into a direct comparative case for skepticism over Christian theism.
Dillahunty concludes that consistent scrutiny has not identified a reliable route to God and argues that a clarity-valuing Jesus could reveal himself directly.
Dillahunty's stated evidential threshold is unrealistically skeptical because even conspicuous, specifically theistic public phenomena would not warrant belief for him.
The move contests the reasonableness of the con side's governing evidential standard and seeks to prevent that standard from controlling the audience's assessment.
Dillahunty's earlier claim that unexplained spectacular phenomena would not uniquely establish that a God caused them.
Hunter characterizes Dillahunty as unconvinced by imagined multilingual lunar writing or an ocean parting in Jesus's name and urges listeners to reject that standard.
General theistic arguments can legitimately support God before resurrection evidence identifies that deity as the Christian God.
The move defends the cumulative architecture connecting generic theism to the debate's specifically Christian conclusion rather than requiring every premise to be uniquely Christian.
Dillahunty's earlier objection that arguments shared with other religions do not establish the specifically Christian God.
Hunter separates his case into generic monotheistic arguments and a resurrection argument, claiming their conjunction supplies the Christian identification.
Divine hiddenness is weakened because substantial evidence for God already exists and God seeks freely chosen trust and loyalty rather than mere compelled intellectual assent.
This directly answers a named central objection by offering both an empirical denial of severe hiddenness and a purpose-based explanation for limited divine manifestation.
Dillahunty's earlier argument that widespread sincere nonbelief disconfirms a God who wants people to know that he exists.
Hunter cites arguments, science, history, philosophy, and experience as available evidence, then says relational freedom may justify God not appearing publicly and irresistibly.
Libertarian freedom is unsupported and conflicts with a creator who knowingly selects a complete universe and whose plan and prophecies fix how events unfold.
The move attacks both the phenomenon supposedly explained by God and the coherence of combining libertarian agency with classical Christian foreknowledge and providence.
Hunter's earlier position that libertarian free choices exist and are best explained by an immaterial divine mind.
Dillahunty denies evidence that anyone could have done otherwise and argues that divine foreknowledge, creation, providential planning, and prophecy are incompatible with libertarian choice.
The Kalam establishes at most that the universe had a cause, while identifying that cause as a transcendent personal God requires unsupported additional assertions.
This directly contests a principal route in the Christian cumulative case by separating the Kalam's stated conclusion from the further inference to God.
Hunter's earlier presentation of the Kalam and its follow-up analysis as evidence supporting a personal transcendent cause.
Dillahunty distinguishes the syllogism from later divine-cause claims, stresses uncertainty about cosmic origins, and argues that invoking God adds no explanatory power.
Supernatural causation has not been confirmably identified, and methods that exclude testable scientific or courtroom scrutiny provide weaker grounds for belief in God.
It supplies the general epistemic standard underlying the skeptical case and challenges whether the proposed evidence can reasonably establish the motion.
Hunter's earlier contention that the available evidence supports God and that divine hiddenness is not a serious evidential obstacle.
Dillahunty contrasts methodological naturalism with inaccessible supernatural explanations and argues that claims unable to withstand reliable evidential scrutiny rest on weaker methods.
The resurrection's proposed minimal facts are not independently confirmable, and scholarly agreement or assessments cannot substitute for the underlying historical data.
This attacks the historical-resurrection route of the cumulative case by disputing both its factual foundation and its appeal to expert consensus.
Hunter's earlier minimal-facts resurrection argument and reliance on assessments across scholars with differing religious commitments.
Dillahunty allows that Jesus likely existed but denies that the crucial resurrection claims are confirmable, emphasizing evidence over the number or sincerity of scholarly opinions.
Extraordinary events would not by themselves identify supernatural agency, but an actually revealing God could provide evidence sufficient to move inquiry from existence to worthiness of worship.
The passage joins the skeptical account of hiddenness to the underdetermination of miraculous evidence, directly addressing whether the Christian God is reasonably established.
Hunter's earlier miraculous hypotheticals and claim that God is not meaningfully hidden from those who assess the available evidence.
Dillahunty says spectacular observations establish only that something occurred, not that God caused it, while maintaining that a genuine deity could make its existence knowable.
Standards of demonstration properly vary with the claim, and an omniscient God could supply convincing evidence without overriding a person's freedom.
This develops the evidential and hiddenness case while answering the objection that skepticism makes belief in God impossible by construction.
Hunter's suggestion that Dillahunty's epistemic framework may prevent any divine act from convincing him unless God removes his freedom.
Dillahunty explains claim-sensitive evidence, distinguishes an initial experience from investigated confirmation, and argues that God would know how to begin a convincing inquiry.
The apparent ability to choose otherwise does not demonstrate libertarian freedom, and available considerations leave determinism open without establishing it conclusively.
This directly contests libertarian freedom, a major premise in Hunter's broader case concerning rational agency, morality, and Christian theism.
Hunter's earlier claim that human choices and beliefs could have been otherwise and therefore support the reality of libertarian freedom.
Dillahunty distinguishes denying freedom from withholding belief in it, invokes the difficulty of testing alternative possibilities, and notes relevant decision-timing research.
Immediate experience makes libertarian freedom more plausible than its denial, and without such freedom genuinely rational affirmation would be impossible.
The move defends the freedom premise that supports Hunter's arguments about rational deliberation and the coherence of responsible belief.
Dillahunty's challenge to distinguish merely feeling able to do otherwise from actually possessing libertarian freedom.
Hunter appeals first to the comparative plausibility of immediate agency experience and then argues that rational affirmation requires a real capacity to select among beliefs.
A deterministic system may produce true outputs, but rational belief requires deliberative selection among reasons and therefore depends on libertarian freedom.
This answers the calculator counterexample and supplies the key conceptual bridge from freedom to rationality in Hunter's case.
Dillahunty's calculator example asserting that a system can reach correct and apparently reasonable conclusions without possessing free will.
Hunter distinguishes a belief's truth from the rational process of reaching it and defines rationality as deliberation that includes choosing against irrational alternatives.
Determinism does not prevent a decision-making agent from revising beliefs in response to new information, so rational change does not require libertarian choice.
This directly rebuts the asserted dependence of rationality on libertarian freedom and preserves the skeptical account of evidence-responsive cognition.
Hunter's claim that rational deliberation is impossible unless an agent has libertarian freedom to choose against irrational beliefs.
Dillahunty describes people as complex decision-making systems whose conclusions can change causally when arguments or evidence supply new inputs.
The Kalam is the beginning rather than the entirety of a cumulative argument for God, and skepticism must still address its causal premise and conclusion before assessing later divine attributes.
This clarifies the intended architecture of the cosmological case and challenges the principal skeptical criticism that the syllogism does not itself name God.
Dillahunty's rebuttal that the Kalam concludes only that the universe has a cause and therefore does not constitute an argument for God.
Hunter says his case begins with the Kalam and proceeds beyond it, then presses whether an uncaused beginning from nothing remains epistemically possible.
No demonstrated methodology reliably supports the existence of any god, whereas scientific methods earn confidence through consistently reliable results.
This establishes the con side's governing evidential standard and directly challenges whether the cumulative Christian case can justify the debate's existence claim.
Hunter's earlier reliance on philosophical reasoning to infer a transcendent cause and ultimately the Christian God.
Dillahunty contrasts admitting uncertainty with unsupported certainty and asks for a method whose reliability can be demonstrated before accepting theism.
Scientific methods are not the only reliable tools of inquiry; philosophy and history can investigate questions outside science's proper detection range.
The move defends the admissibility of the principal methods supporting Hunter's cumulative case and specifically preserves the Kalam route against methodological exclusion.
Dillahunty's demand for a demonstrably reliable method comparable to science before concluding that any god exists.
Hunter uses a metal-detector analogy to argue that one successful instrument cannot exclude realities outside its scope, then identifies philosophy and history as relevant tools.
Even granting that the universe has a cause or explanation, the Kalam argument supplies no justified knowledge about what that cause is.
This attacks the crucial inference from a generic cosmic cause to the attributes, agency, and identity required for Christian theism.
Hunter's claim that Dillahunty had offered no substantive answer to the Kalam-based case for God.
Dillahunty provisionally grants the causal conclusion and argues that apologists then append an unsupported list of claims about the cause's nature.
The cause of all contiguous physical reality must transcend space, time, and matter, and state-to-event causation further supports an agent with libertarian freedom.
The passage supplies the contested bridge from a first cause to a transcendent personal agent, making it indispensable to Hunter's Kalam route to theism.
Dillahunty's objection that a cause of our universe could be another natural reality and that divine attributes are merely asserted.
Hunter argues that any prior physical domain would only extend the explanatory chain, then distinguishes event, state, and state-to-event causation to infer free agency.
Divine foreknowledge does not eliminate libertarian freedom because knowledge is not causal, and God may choose among only those feasible worlds preserving free choices.
This directly defends the internal coherence of Hunter's libertarian-free-will theism against the objection that omniscient creation fixes every human outcome.
The contrary claim that an omniscient creator's prior knowledge and choice of universe are incompatible with genuine libertarian freedom.
Hunter first denies that knowing an act causes it, then invokes possible and feasible worlds to argue that some desired outcomes may be unavailable if freedom is retained.
Faith understood as assurance without adequate evidence is an unreliable epistemology capable of justifying any belief and cannot resolve salvation claims responsibly.
The move challenges a foundational means by which Christian claims are accepted and connects unreliable belief formation to the high-stakes claims of God and salvation.
The audience member's position that God may have intentionally made faith a necessary condition for experiencing or knowing him.
Dillahunty distinguishes confidence from evidence-independent faith, argues that faith can support mutually incompatible or harmful claims, and demands actual reasons instead.
Past events may be assessed without eyewitness participation, but confidence must track the available evidence and the reliability of the reasoning used.
This states the con side's standard for evaluating resurrection-era and miracle testimony, explaining why ordinary historical inference does not license supernatural conclusions.
The audience member's contention that Dillahunty's approach would rule out conclusions about any past event he did not personally witness.
Dillahunty explains evidence-proportioned historical judgment, contrasts ordinary biological inference with walking-on-water claims, and notes the scarcity of verifiable modern miracles.
Recurring medically unexplained healings and the broader documented miracle literature make dismissal of contemporary miracles evidentially premature.
The move counters the claimed decline or absence of miracles and supports the broader Christian historical case by defending supernatural events as live evidential possibilities.
Dillahunty's argument that supernatural evidence is absent and that apparent miracles diminish as investigation and recording capabilities improve.
Hunter cites published miracle research and repeated reports of unexplained healing, concedes that any case may have an unknown natural cause, but argues the pattern remains significant.
The Kalam is not special pleading because only things beginning in time require causes, while a timeless cause of space, time, and matter has no temporal beginning.
This answers the standard who-caused-God objection while consolidating the argument for a timeless, immaterial, powerful, freely acting cause of the universe.
The audience member's charge that exempting a timeless, spaceless God from the Kalam's causal premise constitutes special pleading.
Hunter derives transcendence from the explanandum, invokes agent causation and absence of prior determinism, and limits the need for beginnings to temporal entities.
Christian theism can accommodate apparent supernatural activity in other religions and remains falsifiable through demonstrated internal contradiction or strong contrary historical evidence.
The move addresses rival revelation and whether Hunter's worldview is insulated from disconfirmation, both of which bear directly on Christian theism's comparative reasonableness.
The audience challenge asking what evidence could disconfirm Hunter's Christianity, including supernatural signs associated with another religion.

Hunter interprets rival supernatural phenomena as potentially deceptive, then says contradiction in the divine concept or credible contemporary documents exposing resurrection claims as fraudulent would count strongly against Christianity.
Christian theism is falsifiable because an internal contradiction in the defined God or strong evidence that the resurrection witnesses knowingly lied would undermine it.
This supplies concrete disconfirmation conditions for the Christian case and directly bears on whether Hunter's worldview is insulated from contrary evidence.
The earlier challenge asked what evidence could make Hunter abandon Christianity and suggested that rival supernatural signs might test his commitment.

After allowing that Christian theology can interpret supernatural events in other religions as deceptive, Hunter distinguishes that accommodation from unfalsifiability and identifies conceptual and historical defeaters.
The central disagreement is not willingness to change one's mind but whether the evidence originally used to justify Christian belief is sufficiently reliable.
This reframes the evidential burden from requiring skeptics to disprove Christianity to examining whether the believer's justificatory method warrants confidence at all.
Hunter had argued that Christianity is falsifiable and that he would revise his belief if sufficiently strong conceptual or historical counterevidence appeared.

Dillahunty grants broad agreement about falsifiability and belief revision, then argues that an unreliable evidential measuring method removes warrant even when it does not establish that the resulting belief is false.
Lack of absolute certainty does not defeat rational inquiry because reason provides maximal attainable confidence and practical agents must operate by the stable rules of experienced reality.
This defends the skeptical epistemology underlying Dillahunty's evidential standard against the objection that uncertainty makes persuasion, education, or ordinary action pointless.
An audience question challenged whether admitting uncertainty makes attempts to correct others or require knowledge-based testing pointless.

Dillahunty distinguishes absolute from maximal certainty, appeals to the demonstrated practical reliability of reason, and maintains that even radical skeptical scenarios leave people accountable to the apparent world's operative constraints.
Beliefs, preferences, and attachments are not simply chosen, so humans may be decision-making systems without being perfectly rational or reducible to deliberate calculation.
The move clarifies Dillahunty's account of agency and involuntary belief, directly connecting to the debate's dispute over libertarian freedom and rational belief formation.
The audience question asked whether Dillahunty regards human beings as merely decision-making machines and whether that view differed from his past understanding.

Dillahunty denies that all mental outcomes arise from conscious rational choice, while explaining that emotional attachments can still serve rational cooperative interests within an interdependent social environment.
The received Bible has demonstrable textual alterations, and the absence or presence of such variants is separate from whether its claims are sufficiently supported.
Textual transmission affects the reliability of a principal evidence source for Christianity, while the final distinction prevents textual purity alone from establishing the source's truth.
The audience question challenged or sought clarification of Dillahunty's earlier assertion that the Bible or some of its narratives had been altered.

Dillahunty points to passages absent from earlier manuscripts as clear alterations, notes that significance remains disputed, and separates manuscript variation from his broader assessment of biblical warrant.
The large raw count of New Testament variants exaggerates the textual problem because the differences are distributed across many manuscripts and recognized variants are openly documented.
This protects the New Testament's evidential usefulness by contextualizing variant counts and arguing that known transmission differences do not justify wholesale distrust of the text.
Dillahunty had argued that the modern Bible is clearly altered, citing passages missing from the oldest available manuscripts as examples.

Hunter accepts familiar disputed passages but contextualizes aggregate variation by manuscript volume, emphasizes scholarly disclosure in many Bibles and churches, and argues that alarm over the differences is disproportionate.
Although sweeping claims of biblical corruption are unwarranted, missing originals make textual reliability inferential and some surviving errors may still matter doctrinally.
This qualified rebuttal preserves the skeptical challenge to scriptural reliability while conceding Hunter's point that most textual variants are neither pervasive nor consequential.
Hunter had argued that variant totals are routinely overstated, most recognized differences are disclosed, and the textual alarm is therefore greatly exaggerated.

Dillahunty rejects indiscriminate accusations against the Bible but stresses that reconstruction without originals remains probabilistic, then distinguishes mostly minor variations from a smaller possibility of doctrinally important errors.
